title: Modalyst Pricing: What You Actually Pay in Year One
excerpt: Modalyst advertises a free plan, but the real cost lives in supplier access, per-order pricing, and the tier you upgrade to when a product takes off. A full-year breakdown of what a boutique dropshipping store actually spends.
body: Modalyst advertises a free plan, and that is true as far as it goes, but the free plan pays for itself in a specific way: you get access to the AliExpress catalog with limited supplier curation, and you only pay transaction-level markups on what you sell. The moment a product starts moving, the useful part of Modalyst, which is the curated brand-name supplier catalog, sits behind the paid tiers. Budgeting for year one means understanding which layer you will actually live in by month three.

The pricing structure runs from a free tier up to roughly two hundred thirty-five dollars a month at the top end. The free tier supports a small product count and a slower onboarding flow, which is fine for testing niches, but it hides the two costs that decide your margin: how much the supplier charges per unit and how much you mark the product up to cover the platform, the ads, and the shipping. The subscription fee is rarely the line item that hurts; the per-product economics are.

The real differentiator inside Modalyst is supplier access. Brand-name and boutique suppliers that handle their own warehousing and quality control sit in the paid catalog, and those products carry higher wholesale prices that you pass through with a markup. AliExpress-style sourcing keeps the base cost low but shifts quality control and delivery time onto you. A year-one plan should assume one or two suppliers that match your brand tone, because that is where repeat customers come from.

The practical way to project cost is per SKU, not per month. For a store selling forty units a day from two curated suppliers, the monthly math is roughly the subscription fee, the wholesale unit cost across orders, and the markup that keeps gross margin above forty percent. If the markup collapses under ad cost and shipping, no subscription tier saves you. That is the number to model before you upgrade, not after.

The upgrade triggers are worth naming in advance. When your catalog passes the free plan's product limits, when you need supplier curation for a second niche, or when you want the faster fulfillment promises that paid suppliers carry, the paid tier stops being optional. Each of those triggers should be attached to a revenue milestone, so the fee grows only when the store does.

A useful year-one discipline is to recompute the per-unit margin every month on the three best sellers, because wholesale prices and shipping rates drift. The DTCwise dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the Modalyst page at /tool/modalyst holds the live fee structure, so the monthly recheck stays a ten-minute task.
